questions.prompt: L1: 4 cycles, 80% hit rate. L2: 20 cycles, 50% hit rate (of L1 misses). DRAM: 200 cycles. What's the AMAT in cycles?
In the chapter's example, DRAM is reached only 4% of the time but contributes most of the AMAT. Why?
options: DRAM is accessed in parallel with L1
Its latency is so large that even a small fraction of accesses dominates the average
The L2 hit rate is measured over all accesses
questions.explanation: 0.04 × 300 = 12 cycles out of 17.4. Rare-but-huge costs dominate averages.

questions.prompt: A program walks a linked list whose nodes are scattered randomly across 4 GB of memory. Which describes it best?
questions.explanation: Each load's address depends on the previous load, so only one request can be in flight. Latency, not bandwidth, sets the speed.

questions.prompt: Which CPU mechanisms aim to reduce or hide the latency seen by a single thread?
questions.explanation: Caches, out-of-order execution and prefetching all target one thread's waiting time. More DRAM channels add bandwidth; they don't make any single access faster.

questions.prompt: Why do caches fetch a whole 64-byte line on a miss instead of just the 4 bytes requested?
questions.explanation: Spatial locality: nearby addresses are likely to be used soon, so the rest of the line is probably useful.

questions.prompt: You stream once through a 2 GB array, adding pairs of numbers. Larger caches would…
options: help a lot, because the data is reused
help little, because each byte is used once and the data doesn't fit
questions.explanation: No reuse and no fit: everything comes from DRAM, so the limit is bandwidth (and enough requests in flight).
